rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God lowered and spread the earth over water so its inhabitants could benefit from it; most read al-arḍ in the accusative, while Abū al-Sammāl reads nominative.
rows.anchor: والأرض وضعها للأنام: أي خفضها مدحوة على الماء لينتفع بها. وقرأ الجمهور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets al-anām narrowly as Adam's descendants alone.
rows.anchor: والأنام، قال ابن عباس: بنو آدم فقط

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة وابن زيد والشعبي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, Ibn Zayd, and al-Shaʿbī also define al-anām as every kind of animal.
rows.anchor: وقال أيضا هو وقتادة وابن زيد والشعبي: الحيوان كله

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan takes al-anām to mean the two accountable kinds, jinn and humans.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: الثقلان، الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite mention of fruit begins an ascent from lesser to greater benefits, since fruit is less useful than the items that follow.
rows.anchor: وبدأ بقوله: فاكهة، إذ هو من باب الابتداء بالأدنى والترقي إلى الأعلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence names fruit, palms, grain, and fragrance to include pleasure, staple food for people, fodder for livestock, and pleasant scent.
rows.anchor: ليحصل ما به يتفكه، وما به يتقوت، وما به تقع اللذاذة من الرائحة الطيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The palm tree is named rather than only its fruit because its leaves, fiber, trunk, heart, and fruit all have extensive uses; fruit trees themselves have little value beside their produce.
rows.anchor: لعظم المنفعة بالنخل من جهات متعددة، وشجرة الفاكهة بالنسبة إلى ثمرتها حقيرة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers put al-ḥabb, dhu al-ʿaṣf, and al-rayḥān in the nominative, coordinating them with the preceding nominative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: والحب ذو العصف والريحان، برفع الثلاثة عطفا على المرفوع قبله

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وأبو حيوة وابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Ḥaywa, and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read the three terms in the accusative, with an understood verb meaning God created the grain.
rows.anchor: وابن عامر وأبو حيوة وابن أبي عبلة: بنصب الثلاثة، أي وخلق الحب

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي والأصمعي عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: These readers put al-rayḥān in the genitive, yielding grain as fodder for animals and rayḥān as food for people; the fragrant plant is an unlikely sense in this reading.
rows.anchor: والأصمعي، عن أبي عمرو: والريحان بالجر، والمعنى: والحب ذو العصف الذي هو علف البهائم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī allows rayḥān to be a noun used in place of a verbal noun, or an anomalous verbal noun on the pattern faʿlān.
rows.anchor: وأجاز أبو علي أن يكون اسما، ووضع موضع المصدر، وأن يكون مصدرا على وزن فعلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word rayḥān may reflect an irregular change from the root form rīwḥān, with wāw turned into yāʾ and then deletion of the middle radical, like mayyit and hayyin.
rows.anchor: فأصله ريوحان، قلبت الواو ياء وأدغمت في الياء فصار ريحان، ثم حذفت عين الكلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated question reminds both accountable species that God's blessings cannot be denied and asks which blessing they could deny.
rows.anchor: أي أن نعمه كثيرة لا تحصى، فبأيها تكذبان؟ أي من هذه نعمه لا يمكن أن يكذب بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address is to jinn and humans, who are included in al-anām, supported by the nearby references to human creation, jinn creation, and the address to both species.
rows.anchor: وكان هذا الخطاب للثقلين، لأنهما داخلان في الأنام على أصح الأقوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects as remote the proposal that the address is to men and women among Adam's descendants, and even more strongly rejects addressing one person in the dual form.
rows.anchor: وقد أبعد من جعله خطابا للذكر والأنثى من بني آدم. وأبعد من هذا قول من قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form fa-bi-ayyi is treated as tanwīn after elision of its complement, with ālāʾ as an appositional clarification; ālāʾ means blessings and has several reported singular forms.
rows.anchor: فبأي منونا في جميع السورة، كأنه حذف منه المضاف إليه وأبدل منه آلاء ربكما بدل معرفة من نكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity's creation is introduced after the greater world because humans are the beneficiaries for whom those blessings were created; the majority identify al-insān as Adam.
rows.anchor: ذكر مبدأ من خلقت له هذه النعم، والإنسان هو آدم، وهو قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view takes al-insān generically; this works because the first human was created from clay.
rows.anchor: وقيل: للجنس، وساغ ذلك لأن أباهم مخلوق من الصلصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the verse means Adam, the changing material of his origin—dust, clay, altered mud, then dried clay—explains why creation is attributed to each stage.
rows.anchor: فكان أولا ترابا، ثم طينا، ثم حمأ مسنونا، ثم صلصالا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan identifies al-jānn as the father of the jinn, Iblīs.
rows.anchor: والجان هو أبو الجن، وهو إبليس، قاله الحسن

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid also says al-jānn is the father of the jinn but says he is not Iblīs.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هو أبو الجن، وليس بإبليس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view understands al-jānn as the jinn species collectively.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الجان اسم جنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marij is variously glossed as mixed flame of several colors, flame itself, pure flame, redness at the edge of fire, flame mixed with blackness, or restless smokeless fire.
rows.anchor: والمارج: ما اختلط من أصفر وأحمر وأخضر، أو اللهب، أو الخالص، أو الحمرة في طرف النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first min marks the point of origin, while the second min in min nār is partitive; repetition of the refrain emphasizes, alerts, and stirs, though some attribute it to differing blessings.
rows.anchor: ومن الأولى لابتداء الغاية، والثانية في من نار للتبعيض. وقيل للبيان والتكرار في هذه الفواصل

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba and others explain the repeated refrain as renewed admonition for each distinct blessing.
rows.anchor: وذهب قوم منهم ابن قتيبة إلى أن هذا التكرار إنما هو لاختلاف النعم

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce rabb in the nominative; Abū Ḥaywa and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it in the genitive as an appositive to rabbikumā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: رب، ورب بالرفع، أي هو رب وأبو حيوة وابن أبي عبلة: بالخفض بدلا من ربكما

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid takes the two east points and two west points as the sun's summer and winter rising and setting places.
rows.anchor: وثنى المضاف إليه لأنهما مشرقا الصيف والشتاء ومغرباهما، قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view assigns the two east and west points to the sun and moon.
rows.anchor: وقيل: مشرقا الشمس والقمر ومغرباهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās describes the sun's seasonal east points as a summer ascent and a winter descent, between which it moves.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: للشمس مشرق في الصيف مصعد، ومشرق في الشتاء منحدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further interpretation makes the east points sunrise and dawn, and the west points sunset and twilight.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المشرقان: مطلع الفجر ومطلع الشمس، والمغربان مغرب الشفق ومغرب الشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the esoteric interpretations associated with Sahl al-Tustarī and extremist Sufis as distortions unsupported by Arabic and unintended by God.
rows.anchor: شبيه بكلام الباطنية المحرفين مدلول كلام الله، ضربنا عن ذكره صفحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He defers discussion of the two seas to al-Furqān and reports Ibn ʿAṭiyya's dismissal of al-Thaʿlabī's riddling esoteric interpretations.
rows.anchor: تقدم الكلام على ذلك في الفرقان. قال ابن عطية: وذكر الثعلبي في مرج البحرين ألغازا وأقوالا باطنة لا يلتفت إلى شيء منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense is that the two bodies of water meet and pass one another without a visible boundary; other reports say they meet annually or would meet but for the barrier.
rows.anchor: والظاهر التقاؤهما، أي يتجاوزان، فلا فصل بين الماءين في رؤية العين

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda identifies the barzakh as the bodies of the earth.
rows.anchor: وقيل: البرزخ: أجرام الأرض، قاله قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: La yabghiyān may mean that the waters do not cross their bounds or overpower one another, do not harm people and settlement, or do not seek a different state from the one assigned to them.
rows.anchor: لا يتجاوزان حدهما، ولا يبغي أحدهما على الآخر بالممارجة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya objects that observation does not support fresh river water remaining separate from salt water.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: والعيان لا يقتضيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He proposes that mixing changes the fresh water's constituent bodies, making the whole appear salty to taste.
rows.anchor: وقد يقال: إنه بالاختلاط تتغير أجرام العذب حتى

rows.speaker: القاضي منذر بن سعيد البلوطي
rows.claim: The cited poem says that in mixed waters neither fresh water dominates in taste nor does salt water become fresh.
rows.anchor: وممزوجة الأمواه لا العذب غالب ... على الملح طيبا لا ولا الملح يعذب

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers use the active form yakhruju; Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, and the people of Medina read it passively, while other transmitted forms make God the subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: يخرج مبنيا للفاعل ونافع وأبو عمرو وأهل المدينة: مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash reports the view that pearls and coral emerge from both fresh and salt waters; critics reject it because experience finds them only in salt water.
rows.anchor: وقال بذلك قوم، حكاه الأخفش. ورد الناس هذا القول، قالوا: والحس يخالفه

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority say pearls form in salt water near river mouths, so the verse attributes them to both waters; divers commonly know this account.
rows.anchor: وقال الجمهور: إنما يخرج من الأجاج في المواضع التي تقع فيها الأنهار والمياه العذبة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrima say the rain enters the sea and opens the shells, accounting for the attribution to both waters.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وعكرمة: تكون هذه الأشياء في البحر بنزول المطر

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says pearls come only from salt water, with the reference to both waters understood figuratively.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: إنما يخرج من الملح، لكنه قال منهما تجوزا

rows.speaker: الرماني
rows.claim: Al-Rummānī compares fresh water's role to a male's in fertilization, allowing the offspring to be attributed to both parents.
rows.anchor: وقال الرماني: العذب فيها كاللقاح للملح

rows.speaker: ابن عطية والزجاج
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya, followed by al-Zajjāj, treats fresh and salt water as one kind collectively, although the products may belong in detail to only one part.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية، وتبع الزجاج من حيث هما نوع واحد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the waters become like one body on meeting, just as something taken from one neighborhood can be said to come from a city; another view locates the products only at their meeting point.
rows.anchor: لما التقيا وصارا كالشيء الواحد، جاز أن يقال: يخرجان منهما

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī parses the phrase as ellipsis of a noun, meaning that the products emerge from one of the two waters.
rows.anchor: هذا من باب حذف المضاف، والتقدير: يخرج من أحدهما

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī argues that God's wording should be accepted over a human claim that pearls cannot emerge in fresh water, since hidden underwater events may escape even experienced travelers.
rows.anchor: كلام الله تعالى أولى بالاعتبار من كلام بعض الناس، ومن أعلم أن اللؤلؤ لا يخرج من الماء العذب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Qatāda call the larger pearls luʾluʾ and the smaller ones marjān.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والضحاك وقتادة: كبار الجوهر والمرجان صغاره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعلي ومرة الهمداني
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās, as well as ʿAlī and Murra al-Hamdānī, reverses the size distinction.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أيضا، وعلي ومرة الهمداني عكس هذا

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله وأبو مالك
rows.claim: Abū ʿAbd Allāh and Abū Mālik identify coral as red stone, while al-Zajjāj calls it intensely white stone and Abū Yaʿlā says it is a kind of pearl.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله وأبو مالك: المرجان: الحجر الأحمر. وقال الزجاج: حجر شديد البياض

rows.speaker: ابن دريد
rows.claim: Ibn Durayd says marjān is an Arabized foreign word for which he has no inflected usage; al-Aʿshā's verse may mean a large pearl.
rows.anchor: والمرجان: اسم أعجمي معرب. قال ابن دريد: لم أسمع فيه نقل متصرف

rows.speaker: طلحة
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa reads luʾluʾa with a kasra on the third lām, a dialect form; ʿAbd al-Walī reads the final hamza as yāʾ after a kasra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة: اللؤلؤة بكسر اللام الثالثة، وهي لغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ships are specially ascribed to God although people build them because their full usefulness depends on God, who is their true owner.
rows.anchor: لما كانوا هم منشئيها، أسندها تعالى إليه، إذ كان تمام منفعتها إنما هو منه تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-jawārī means ships, while ʿAbd Allāh, al-Ḥasan, and transmitters from Abū ʿAmr read the rāʾ with ḍamma, as in shāk.
rows.anchor: والجواري: السفن. وقرأ عبد الله والحسن وعبد الوارث، عن أبي عمرو: بضم الراء

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid distinguishes ships with raised sails as al-munshaʾāt from those without raised sails.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: ما له شراع من المنشآت، وما لم يرفع له شراع، فليس من المنشآت

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers use munshaʾāt with fatḥa, understood as ships made by God or people, or as ships with raised sails; a kasra reading means ships that raise sails, make waves, or initiate voyages.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور المنشآت بفتح الشين، اسم مفعول: أي أنشأها الله، أو الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ships are compared with mountains to convey their great size, though the word can include vessels large and small; the quoted verse illustrates feminine agreement for the adjective.
rows.anchor: كالأعلام: أي كالجبال والآكام، وهذا يدل على كبر السفن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The collective expression all who are on it uses a masculine pronoun because rational beings predominate; the pronoun refers back to the earth mentioned earlier.
rows.anchor: وعبر بمن في قوله: كل من عليها تغليبا لمن يعقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Perishing means the extinction of every created thing, while face denotes a thing's reality; God is exempt from bodily limbs.
rows.anchor: والفناء عبارة عن إعدام جميع الموجودات من حيوان وغيره، والوجه يعبر به عن حقيقة الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh poor used face idiomatically to ask where a generous Arab was who would give them aid.
rows.anchor: وتقول صعاليك مكة: أين وجه عربي كريم يجود علي

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers use dhū with wāw as an adjective for wajh; Abū and ʿAbd Allāh read dhī with yāʾ as an adjective for the Lord.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: ذو بالواو، وصفة للوجه وأبي وعبد الله: ذي بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent addressee in your Lord's face is the Prophet, which specially honors him; another view makes the address general to every listener.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الخطاب في قوله: وجه ربك للرسول، وفيه تشريف عظيم له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-jalāl is explained as the one whom monotheists exalt above likeness to creation and their deeds, the one whose majesty inspires awe, or the giver of majesty and honor to sincere servants.
rows.anchor: ومعنى ذو الجلال: الذي يجله الموحدون عن التشبيه بخلقه وعن أفعالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everyone in heaven and earth asks God for needs: religious matters for heavenly beings and worldly and religious needs for earthly beings.
rows.anchor: أي حوائجهم، وهو ما يتعلق بمن في السموات من أمر الدين

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abū Ṣāliḥ assigns mercy to the inhabitants of heaven and forgiveness and provision to those on earth.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو صالح: من في السموات: الرحمة، ومن في الأرض: المغفرة والرزق

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says angels ask provision for earthly people and forgiveness, while earthly people ask for both.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: الملائكة الرزق لأهل الأرض والمغفرة، وأهل الأرض يسألونهما جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He takes yasʾaluhu as an independent statement; construing it as a circumstantial clause attached to the face is remote, and even those who do not ask express need implicitly.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: يسأله استئناف إخبار. وقيل: حال من الوجه، والعامل فيه يبقى

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
rows.claim: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr says God answers a caller, frees a captive, accepts a people's repentance, and forgives others.
rows.anchor: وقال عبيد بن عمير: يجيب داعيا، ويفك عانيا، ويتوب على قوم، ويغفر لقوم

rows.speaker: سويد بن غفلة
rows.claim: Suwayd ibn Ghafla summarizes God's acts as freeing slaves, giving the humbled what they need, and plunging people into punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال سويد بن غفلة: يعتق رقابا، ويعطي رغاما ويقحم عقابا

rows.speaker: ابن عيينة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUyayna distinguishes the world's day, with commands, prohibition, death, and life, from the Resurrection day of recompense and reckoning.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عيينة: الدهر عند الله يومان، أحدهما اليوم الذي هو مدة الدنيا

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says the verse was revealed about Jews who claimed that God does nothing on the Sabbath.
rows.anchor: وعن مقاتل: نزلت في اليهود، فقالوا: إن الله لا يقضي يوم السبت شيئا

rows.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
rows.claim: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl reconciles the dried pen and ongoing divine activity by saying God brings forth new affairs rather than beginning new ones.
rows.anchor: شؤون يبديها، لا شؤون يبتديها

rows.speaker: ابن بحر
rows.claim: Ibn Baḥr says the world's day is for testing and the Resurrection day for recompense.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن بحر: هو في يوم الدنيا في الابتلاء، وفي يوم القيامة في الجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kulla yawmin is an adverb governed by the understood stable predicate in fī shaʾn, as in the construction yawm al-jumʿa Zayd qāʾim.
rows.anchor: وانتصب كل يوم على الظرف، والعامل فيه العامل في قوله: في شأن، وهو مستقر المحذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: We shall attend to you means God will take account of people at Resurrection, not that He had prior work to finish; the threat idiom means focusing on punishment.
rows.anchor: أي ننظر في أموركم يوم القيامة، لا أنه تعالى كان له شغل فيفرغ منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic threat I shall free myself for you means that the speaker will set other concerns aside to concentrate on bringing punishment.
rows.anchor: سأفرغ لك، أي سأتجرد للإيقاع بك من كل ما شغلني عنه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows a threat of punishment in this world but regards the Resurrection interpretation as clearer.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون التوعد بعذاب في الدنيا، والأول أبين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the world's affairs end, leaving only judgment, which is metaphorically described as God becoming free to attend to people.
rows.anchor: فلا يبقى إلا شأن واحد وهو جزاؤكم، فجعل ذلك فراغا لهم على طريق المثل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Linguists generally use faragha for finishing a task; a claimed sense of intending is supported by poetry and reports in which the word means to turn one's attention toward someone.
rows.anchor: أن فرغ تستعمل عند انقضاء الشغل الذي كان الإنسان مشتغلا به

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers use first-person plural with ḍamma on rāʾ; other readings vary person, vowel, and passive voice, reflecting dialect forms of faragha.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: سنفرغ بنون العظمة وضم الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two weighty kinds are called thaqalān because they weigh upon earth, bear sins, or because humans are heavy and jinn are named by association.
rows.anchor: والثقلان: الإنس والجن، سميا بذلك لكونهما ثقيلين على وجه الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address to jinn and humans appears to be God's speech to them on Resurrection Day; another view treats it as something said to them then, while a third makes it a worldly warning about escaping death.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: يا معشر الآية من خطاب الله إياهم يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the terrified creatures flee across the earth, find angels surrounding it, and return to their starting point.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: يفرون في أقطار الأرض لما يرون من الهول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads the challenge as asking whether thought and intellect can penetrate and learn the regions of heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: إن استطعتم بأذهانكم وفكركم، أن تنفذوا، فتعلمون علم أقطار

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī interprets the challenge as escape from God's decree and dominion, which is impossible without power and conquest.
rows.anchor: إن استطعتم أن تهربوا من قضائي، وتخرجوا من ملكوتي ومن سمائي وأرضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to break through is a challenge that demonstrates their inability; Qatāda interprets the required sulṭān as sovereignty, which they lack.
rows.anchor: فانفذوا: أمر تعجيز. وقال قتادة: السلطان هنا الملك، وليس لهم ملك

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk also describes markets in which the sky opens and angels descend, surrounding fleeing humans and jinn.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك أيضا: بينما الناس في أسواقهم، انفتحت السماء ونزلت الملائكة

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads the challenge in the dual, addressing the two kinds; most readers use the plural because each kind contains many individuals.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: إن استطعتما، على خطاب تثنية الثقلين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says a flame drives the jinn and humans from their graves toward the gathering place.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: إذا خرجوا من قبورهم، ساقهم شواظ إلى المحشر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid defines shawāẓ as detached red flame, while al-Ḍaḥḥāk calls it smoke issuing from flame.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: اللهب الأحمر المنقطع. وقال الضحاك: الدخان الذي يخرج من اللهب

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce shawāẓ with ḍamma on shīn; ʿĪsā, Ibn Kathīr, and Shibl use kasra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: شواظ، بضم الشين وعيسى وابن كثير وشبل: بكسرها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جبير والنحاس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Naḥḥās take nuḥās as smoke; Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid also report that it means familiar copper.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وابن جبير والنحاس: الدخان وعن ابن عباس أيضا ومجاهد: هو الصفر المعروف

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads the verb in the first-person plural and puts shawāẓ and nuḥās in the accusative as its objects.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: نرسل بالنون، عليكما شواظا بالنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge means the two kinds would be unable to resist if such a punishment were sent against them.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: يعجز الجن والإنس، أي أنتما بحال من يرسل عليه هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer to when the sky splits is omitted to signal the enormity of the terror; its splitting is its rupture at Resurrection.
rows.anchor: فإذا انشقت السماء: جواب إذا محذوف، أي فما أعظم الهول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وأبو صالح
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Ṣāliḥ compare the sky's color to a reddish horse, with feminine agreement because sky is feminine.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وأبو صالح: هي من لون الفرس الورد، فأنث لكون السماء مؤنثة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the sky is blue now but becomes rose-red at that time; al-Zajjāj treats ward as the familiar flower's color.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: هي اليوم زرقاء، ويومئذ تغلب عليها الحمرة كلون الورد

rows.speaker: أبو الجوزاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Jawzāʾ says the sky will be yellow and supports this by noting that Arabs call certain horses ward.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الجوزاء: وردة صفراء. وقال: أما سمعت العرب تسمي الخيل الورد

rows.speaker: الفراء والكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and al-Kalbī compare the changing sky to ward-colored horses, which vary from yellow to red to gray with seasons and cold.
rows.anchor: فشبه تلون السماء بتلون الوردة من الخيل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains al-dihān as red leather; other interpretations compare the sky to differently colored oils, pure oil, or molten, rotating, gleaming oil.
rows.anchor: كالدهان، قال ابن عباس: الأديم الأحمر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī understands al-dihān as olive oil, or a collective term for oil or something used for anointing; cited poetry supports the comparison.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: كالدهان: كدهن الزيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tanwīn in fayaumʾidhin replaces a deleted clause, meaning the day when the sky split; the verse's negation of questioning is reconciled with verses affirming questions in different ways.
rows.anchor: فيومئذ: التنوين فيه للعوض من الجملة المحذوفة، والتقدير: فيوم إذ انشقت السماء

rows.speaker: عكرمة وقتادة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and Qatāda say questioning occurs at some stations but not others.
rows.anchor: فقال عكرمة وقتادة: هي مواطن يسأل في بعضها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās distinguishes questions of rebuke and confirmation from genuine inquiry about a sin, which God already knows.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: حيث ذكر السؤال فهو سؤال توبيخ وتقرير، وحيث نفي فهو استخبار محض

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says questioning happened first, then mouths were sealed and hands and feet testified to people's deeds.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة أيضا: كانت مسألة، ثم ختم على الأفواه وتكلمت الأيدي والأرجل

rows.speaker: أبو العالية وقتادة
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya and Qatāda say an innocent person is not asked about a sinner's wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية وقتادة: لا يسأل غير المجرم عن ذنب المجرم

rows.speaker: الحسن وعمرو بن عبيد
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd use an anomalous hamza reading in jānn to avoid the meeting of two silent letters.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وعمرو بن عبيد: ولا جأن بالهمز

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan identifies sinners' distinguishing marks as blackened faces and blue eyes; the author also allows blindness, muteness, deafness, or other disfigurement.
rows.anchor: وسيما المجرمين: سواد الوجوه وزرقة العيون، قاله الحسن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says sinners are seized by forelock and feet, trampled together like firewood, and cast into the fire.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يؤخذ بناصيته وقدميه فيوطأ، ويجمع كالحطب

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says forelock and feet are joined behind the sinner's back with a chain.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: يجمع بينهما في سلسلة من وراء ظهره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other accounts say angels alternately take sinners by the forelock or feet, or drag different people by one or the other; the passive grammar omits the agent and object.
rows.anchor: وقيل: تسحبهم الملائكة، تارة تأخذ بالنواصي، وتارة بالأقدام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The announcement this is Hell is spoken to sinners to rebuke and reproach them; they circulate between fire and boiling liquid punishment.
rows.anchor: هذه جهنم: أي يقال لهم ذلك على طريق التوبيخ والتقريع. يطوفون بينها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readings vary between passive yutāfūn, an intensive active form, a reflexive form, and the common active yطūfūn, all describing circulation between punishments.
rows.anchor: وقرأ علي والسلمي: يطافون والأعمش وطلحة وابن مقسم

rows.speaker: ابن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr says the promise of two gardens was revealed concerning Abū Bakr.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الزبير: نزلت في أبي بكر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid construes maqām rabbihi as God's standing watch over every person, so the servant refrains from sin; he links the phrase with Q 13:33.
rows.anchor: أي قيام ربه عليه، وهو مروي عن مجاهد، قال: من قوله: أفمن هو قائم على كل نفس بما كسبت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes maqām the place where people stand before their Lord for judgment, highlighting the ordeal; it is linked to Q 83:6.
rows.anchor: الذي يقف فيه العباد للحساب، من قوله: يوم يقوم الناس لرب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further idiom takes maqām as a side or person, so the phrase means whoever fears his Lord.
rows.anchor: مقام مقحم، والمعنى: ولمن خاف ربه، كما تقول: أخاف جانب فلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning gives each individual who fears God two gardens; proposed explanations include a home and one for family, Eden and Bliss, two alternating homes, or one each for jinn and humans.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن لكل فرد فرد من الخائفين جنتان، قيل: إحداهما منزله، والأخرى لأزواجه وخدمه

rows.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري
rows.claim: Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī assigns a garden of gold to the foremost and a garden of silver to their followers.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو موسى الأشعري: جنة من ذهب للسابقين، وجنة من فضة للتابعين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī suggests one garden for performing duties and another for avoiding sins, or a night's lodging and a further garden granted as favor.
rows.anchor: جنة لفعل الطاعات، وجنة لترك المعاصي، لأن التكليف دائر عليهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afnān means branching limbs, singled out because they leaf, bear fruit, cast shade, and provide fruit for picking.
rows.anchor: وخص الأفنان بالذكر جمع فنن، وهي الغصون التي تتشعب عن فروع الشجر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the fruit can be gathered standing, sitting, or reclining, without withdrawing the hand far or encountering thorns.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: تجتنيه قائما وقاعدا ومضطجعا، لا يرد يده بعد ولا شوك

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: ʿĪsā reads jannā with fatḥa on jīm and kasra on nūn; another reading has kasra on jīm.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى: بفتح الجيم وكسر النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in fīhinna may refer to the many gardens implied when every individual has two, or to the furnishings and chambers inside them if only two gardens are meant.
rows.anchor: والضمير في فيهن عائد على الجنان الدال عليهن جنتان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says fīhinna encompasses the blessings just listed, including the gardens, springs, fruit, and gathered produce; Abū Ḥayyān finds this remote.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: فيهن في هذه الآلاء المعدودة من الجنتين والعينين والفاكهة والجنى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says each location within Paradise is itself a garden, explaining the plural pronoun.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: كل موضع من الجنة جنة، فلذلك قال: فيهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭarf is originally a verbal noun, which accounts for its singular form.
rows.anchor: والطرف أصله مصدر، فلذلك وحد

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the women confine their gaze to their husbands, with one telling her husband that by God's honor she sees no one more handsome in Paradise.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: تقول لزوجها: وعزة ربي ما أرى في الجنة أحسن منك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the women are so beautiful that they make anyone looking at them avert his eyes from all others.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الطرف طرف غيرهن، أي قصرن عيني من ينظر إليهن عن النظر إلى غيرهن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says lam yaṭmithhunna means no husband has deflowered them; ʿIkrima broadens it to exclude intercourse of any kind.
rows.anchor: لم يطمثهن، قال ابن عباس: لم يفتضهن قبل أزواجهن

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers use kasra on the mīm in both occurrences; other named readers vary the vowel, and al-Jaḥdarī uses fatḥa in both.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: بكسر ميم يطمثهن في الموضعين

rows.speaker: مجاهد والحسن
rows.claim: Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan say human women may have intercourse with their human partners, but the verse denies all previous partners because God does not specify husbands.
rows.anchor: فقال مجاهد والحسن: قد تجامع نساء البشر مع أزواجهن، إذ لم يذكر الزوج الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ضمرة بن حبيب
rows.claim: Ḍamra ibn Ḥabīb says jinn in Paradise have their own jinn women, so the verse denies prior intercourse with human and jinn women alike.
rows.anchor: قال ضمرة بن حبيب: الجن في الجنة لهم قاصرات الطرف من الجن نوعهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda compares the women to clear ruby and red coral: a thread placed inside a ruby can be seen through it.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: كأنهن على صفاء الياقوت وحمرة المرجان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Tirmidhī report says the marrow of a Paradise woman's leg can be seen through seventy layers of clothing.
rows.anchor: وفي الترمذي: أن المرأة من نساء الجنة ليرى بياض ساقها من وراء سبعين حلة مخها

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says ruby evokes smoothness and translucence while coral evokes smoothness and beauty; Arabic women were named with pearl and coral terms.
rows.anchor: فالياقوت في إملاسه وشفوفه، والمرجان في إملاسه وجمال منظره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reward for excellence in deeds is excellence in recompense; another view limits the excellence to monotheism and its reward, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq reads al-ḥusān as houris.
rows.anchor: هل جزاء الإحسان في العمل، إلا الإحسان في الثواب؟ وقيل: هل جزاء التوحيد إلا الجنة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد والأكثرون
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and most exegetes say the two gardens mentioned later are lower in rank and belong to the people of the right, while the first pair belongs to the foremost.
rows.anchor: لأصحاب اليمين، والأوليان هما للسابقين، قاله ابن زيد والأكثرون

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the first pair is for the foremost and the second pair for the followers.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: الأوليان للسابقين، والأخريان للتابعين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the later gardens are closer to their beneficiaries but superior to the first pair; al-Zamakhsharī favors this reading.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: ومن دونهما في القرب للمنعمين، والمؤخرتا الذكر أفضل من الأوليين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supporters of the first ranking cite the first pair's flowing springs, greater abundance of fruit, brocade-lined couches rather than canopies, finer silk, and ruby-and-coral description.
rows.anchor: ورجح غيره القول الأول بذكر جري العينين والنضخ دون الجري

rows.speaker: ابن هرمز
rows.claim: Ibn Hurmuz reads khudr with ḍamma on ḍād, a rare dialect also illustrated by poetry using plural forms for red and yellow.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن هرمز: خضر بضم الضاد. قال صاحب اللوامح: وهي لغة قليلة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers make dhu al-jalāl an adjective for rabb; Ibn ʿĀmir and the Syrians make dhaw an adjective for the name, with further variant forms transmitted.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: ذي الجلال: صفة لربك وابن عامر وأهل الشام: ذو صفة للاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here al-ism means the named entity; another view treats the word name as redundant, as face may be in the verse about the Lord's face.
rows.anchor: والمراد هنا بالاسم المسمى. وقيل: اسم مقحم، كالوجه في ويبقى وجه ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blessing can be predicated of the name as elevation; if the name is elevated, the named Lord is all the more worthy of elevation.
rows.anchor: وقد صح الإسناد إلى الاسم لأنه بمعنى العلو، فإذا علا الاسم، فما ظنك بالمسمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending of worldly blessings with the enduring face matches the end of afterlife blessings with the blessed name: permanence suits the world's passing, while growth suits the increase and duration of Paradise's gifts.
rows.anchor: ختم تعالى نعم الدنيا بقوله: ويبقى وجه ربك ذو الجلال والإكرام، ختم نعم الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet taught people to invoke God by the name dhu al-jalāl wa-l-ikrām.
rows.anchor: قال صلى الله عليه وسلم: «ألظوا بيا ذا الجلال والإكرام»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is Meccan and follows the previous surah's mention of the fortunate, the wretched, and deniers by describing Resurrection and its rewards and punishments, with past destroyed peoples as warnings to Meccans.
rows.anchor: هذه السورة مكية. ومناسبتها لما قبلها: أنه لما ذكر شيئا من أحوال السعداء والأشقياء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others identify al-ḥāqqah as Resurrection and resurrection, when every worker meets the consequence of his deeds.
rows.anchor: الحاقة: المراد بها القيامة والبعث، قاله ابن عباس وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations say it reveals realities, names the time when matters become real, or is an active participle from ḥaqqa, meaning something firmly established and beyond doubt.
rows.anchor: لأنها تبدي حقائق الأشياء. وقيل: سميت بذلك لأن الأمر يحق فيها

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azharī explains the root through competition: the Resurrection is al-ḥāqqah because it defeats every opponent of God's religion who argues falsely.
rows.anchor: وقال الأزهري: حاققته فحققته أحقه: أي غالبته فغلبته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further analysis treats al-ḥāqqah as a verbal noun like al-ʿāqibah.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الحاقة مصدر كالعاقبة والعافية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated noun links the two clauses: al-ḥāqqah is the first subject, mā the second subject, and al-ḥāqqah its predicate; mā is an awe-inspiring question rather than a genuine inquiry.
rows.anchor: والحاقة مبتدأ، وما مبتدأ ثان، والحاقة خبره، والجملة خبر عن الحاقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the subject intensifies the grandeur and dread of the event; the construction commonly uses repetition when emphasizing or magnifying something.
rows.anchor: وما استفهام لا يراد حقيقته بل التعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What could make you know what the Resurrection is heightens the warning: its ordeals exceed what anyone could know or describe.
rows.anchor: وما أدراك ما الحاقة: مبالغة في التهويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root darā normally takes bi, sometimes omitted; with the causative hamza the two objects take different constructions, so mā al-ḥāqqah is accusative after the omitted preposition.
rows.anchor: وأصل درى أن يعدى بالباء، وقد تحذف على قلة، فإذا دخلت همزة النقل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says al-qāriʿah is a name for Resurrection because it strikes hearts, people, sky, earth, mountains, and stars with its shocks.
rows.anchor: تقرع القلوب بصدمتها. وقال الزمخشري: تقرع الناس بالأقراع والأهوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling it al-qāriʿah foregrounds the striking that intensifies the description of al-ḥāqqah; the account of destroyed deniers warns Meccans against repeating their fate.
rows.anchor: فوضع الضمير ليدل على معنى القرع في الحاقة زيادة في وصف شدتها

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers use the passive form fa-uhlikū; Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads the verb as active, fa-halakū.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: فأهلكوا: رباعيا مبنيا للمفعول وزيد بن علي: فهلكوا مبنيا للفاعل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda explains al-ṭāghiyah as a cry beyond the bounds of any ordinary cry.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: بالطاغية: بالصيحة التي خرجت عن حد كل صيحة

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن زيد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd say the term means the tyrannical deed they committed.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وابن زيد: بسبب الفعلة الطاغية التي فعلوها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن زيد وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Zayd, and Abū ʿUbayda parse al-ṭāghiyah as a verbal noun meaning their tyranny.
rows.anchor: مصدر كالعاقبة، فكأنه قال: بطغيانهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other possibilities are the she-camel's killer, with the whole people destroyed for approving it, or a tyrannical faction; al-Ṭabarī prefers the cry because it parallels Aad's destructive wind.
rows.anchor: واختار الطبري وغيره أن الطاغية هي الصيحة، وترجيح ذلك مقابلة سبب الهلاك في ثمود بسبب الهلاك في عاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aad's wind is called ʿātiyah because it defied its keepers, overcame Aad so they could not shelter, or metaphorically because it blew violently.
rows.anchor: عتت على خزانها فخرجت بغير مقدار، أو على عاد فما قدروا على أن يتستروا منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taskhīr means using something with power; here the wind was kept over Aad and made to persist for seven nights.
rows.anchor: والتسخير هو استعمال الشيء باقتدار عليه. فمعنى سخرها عليهم: أي أقامها وأدامها

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd derives the term from decisive cutting: the days cut the people down as a disease is checked or severed.
rows.anchor: حسوما جمع حاسم، أي تلك الأيام قطعتهم بالإهلاك، ومنه حسم العلل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī offers three parses for ḥusūman: an omitted verb meaning it exterminated them, an adjective meaning possessed of destructive force, or a purpose clause.
rows.anchor: أي تحسم حسوما بمعنى تستأصل استئصالا، أو تكون صفة، كقولك: ذات حسوم

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī reads ḥusūman with fatḥa as a circumstantial description of the wind, meaning it was exterminating.
rows.anchor: وقرأ السدي: حسوما بالفتح: حالا من الريح، أي سخرها عليهم مستأصلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase fatarā al-qawma fīhā may locate them in the nights and days, their homes, or the wind's path; he prefers the first as nearest and explicit.
rows.anchor: أظهرها الأول لأنه أقرب ومصرح به

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash records a reading nukhayl khāwiyah, whose hollow trunks are empty through decay and ruin.
rows.anchor: وحكى الأخفش أنه قرىء: نخيل خاوية خلت أعجازها بلى وفسادا

rows.speaker: ابن شجرة
rows.claim: Ibn Shajara says the wind entered their mouths and expelled what was inside them through their backs, leaving them like hollow palms.
rows.anchor: كانت تدخل من أفواههم فتخرج ما في أجوافهم من الحسو من أدبارهم

rows.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Sallām says their bodies became hollow of their spirits.
rows.anchor: وقال يحيى بن سلام: خلت أبدانهم من أرواحهم

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the people suffered for seven days, died on the eighth, and the wind cast them into the sea, explaining whether any remained.
rows.anchor: كانوا في سبعة أيام في عذاب، ثم في الثامن ماتوا وألقتهم الريح في البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min bāqiyah may mean any surviving person or faction, or a feminine intensive form, or the verbal noun baqāʾ on the pattern fāʿilah.
rows.anchor: من باقية: أي من باق، والهاء للمبالغة. وقال أيضا: من فئة باقية

rows.speaker: الجمهور وأبو جعفر وشيبة والسلمي
rows.claim: Most readers and several authorities take min qablihi temporally, meaning earlier unbelieving nations such as Noah's people.
rows.anchor: وقرأ باقي السبعة وأبو جعفر وشيبة والسلمي: ومن قبله، ظرف زمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A kasra reading of qablihi is spatial, meaning Pharaoh's supporters and people in his vicinity; al-muʾtafikāt are Lot's towns, and al-khāṭiʾah means wrongful acts or error.
rows.anchor: أي أجناده وأهل طاعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rasūl is collective and means each messenger sent by God; other views identify Lot because he is nearest in context or Moses because he appears earlier, and it may mean a message.
rows.anchor: فعصوا رسول ربهم: رسول جنس، وهو من جاءهم من عند الله تعالى

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says rابيَة means severe, exceeding other acts of seizure such as drowning or overturning the towns.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: شديدة، يريد أنها زادت على غيرها من الأخذات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flood rose fifteen cubits above the world's highest mountain; Ibn Jubayr says it overpowered the flood's keepers as the wind overpowered its keepers.
rows.anchor: أي زاد وعلا على أعلى جبل في الدنيا خمس عشرة ذراعا

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr says the water overpowered its keepers just as the destructive wind did.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جبير: طغى على الخزان، كما طغت الريح على خزانها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural second-person pronoun refers to later descendants carried in their forefathers' loins aboard Noah's ark; jāriyah became a common word for a ship.
rows.anchor: حملناكم: أي في أصلاب آبائكم، في الجارية: هي سفينة نوح عليه السلام

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī reads the phrase broadly as ships sailing, a divine favor whose human beneficiaries are the addressed audience.
rows.anchor: وقال المهدوي: المعنى في السفن الجارية يعني أن ذلك هو على سبيل الامتنان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ark is a reminder and admonition of Noah's people, distinguishing those who perished from those who were saved; an alternate view makes the whole event a lesson about ancestral rescue and the drowning of deniers.
rows.anchor: أي سفينة نوح عليه السلام، لكم تذكرة بما جرى لقومه الهالكين وقومه الناجين

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the ark's remains were seen by the earliest generations of this community; Ibn Jurayj says its planks were on al-Jūdī.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: أدركها أوائل هذه الأمة. وقال ابن جريج: كانت ألواحها على الجودي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An attentive ear is one disposed to understand and preserve admonitions; waʿaytu is used for retaining something in the self, while awʿaytu is for putting something in a container.
rows.anchor: يقال: وعيت لما حفظ في النفس، وأوعيت لما حفظ في غير النفس من الأوعية

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the attentive ear has understood God and benefited from what it hears of the Book.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: الواعية هي التي عقلت عن الله وانتفعت بما سمعت من كتاب الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophetic report says the Prophet prayed that ʿAlī's ear would be made attentive; ʿAlī said he thereafter forgot nothing he heard.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث، أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم قال لعلي: «إني دعوت الله تعالى أن يجعلها أذنك يا علي»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A transmitted doubled yāʾ is called erroneous, but may be understood as emphatic articulation rather than true gemination or a pause reading extended into connected speech.
rows.anchor: قيل: وهو خطأ وينبغي أن يتأول على أنه أريد به شدة بيان الياء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the singular indefinite attentive ear signals the scarcity of people who understand God, rebukes the many who do not, and makes one truly attentive person the majority in God's regard; Abū Ḥayyān calls this excessive.
rows.anchor: وللدلالة على أن الأذن الواحدة إذا وعت وعقلت عن الله تعالى فهي السواد الأعظم عند الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning worldly destruction of the messengers' deniers, the passage turns to the afterlife and begins with the event of the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر تعالى ما فعل بمكذبي الرسل من العذاب في الدنيا، ذكر أمر الآخرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the single blast as the first blast that brings about the world's destruction, supported by the following carrying of earth and mountains.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: وهي النفخة الأولى التي يحصل عنها خراب العالم

rows.speaker: ابن المسيب ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn al-Musayyab and Muqātil identify it as the final blast; on that view the mountains are not crushed after the blast, since conjunction does not establish sequence.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن المسيب ومقاتل: هي النفخة الآخرة، وعلى هذا لا يكون الدك بعد النفخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word wāḥidah emphasizes that the blast occurs once; the majority raise both words, while Abū al-Sammāl uses the accusative with the prepositional phrase as passive subject.
rows.anchor: ولما كانت مرة أكدت بقوله: واحدة. وقرأ الجمهور: نفخة واحدة، برفعهما

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the adjective permits rafʿ; Abū Ḥayyān replies that a bounded verbal noun would remain nominative even without the adjective, which only emphasizes it.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: لما نعت صح رفعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A light reading of ḥummilat makes the earth and mountains carried by a violent wind, angels, or divine power; an earthquake is unlikely because shaking does not carry.
rows.anchor: فالتخفيف على أن تكون الأرض والجبال حملتها الريح العاصف أو الملائكة أو القدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dual pronoun in fudakkatā refers to earth and mountains as two wholes; they are struck together and fragmented, while dakk can also mean flattened into an even plain.
rows.anchor: وثني الضمير في فدكتا، وإن كان قد تقدمه ما يعود عليه ضمير الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dakk suggests separating fragments, as in the image of dust; daqq suggests a differing division of particles, while another explanation says the earth becomes level without rises or hollows.
rows.anchor: والدك فيه تفرق الأجزاء لقوله: هباء ، والدق فيه اختلاف الأجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fayawmaʾidhin coordinates with the conditional clause and is governed by waqaʿat; the tanwīn compensates for the omitted sequence of events after the blast.
rows.anchor: والتنوين في إذ للعوض من الجملة المحذوفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The waqiʿah is Resurrection; an earlier discussion also reports the view that it is a rock at Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: والواقعة هي القيامة، وقد تقدم في إذا وقعت الواقعة أن بعضهم قال: هي صخرة بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky splits apart and becomes weak after having been firm; wāhiyah may also mean torn open like a leaking waterskin.
rows.anchor: وانشقت السماء: أي انفطرت وتميز بعضها من بعض، فهي يومئذ انشقت، واهية: ضعيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations say the sky splits to admit descending angels or from the terror of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقيل انشقاقها لنزول الملائكة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās locates the angels on the edges of the sky as it splits.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: على حافاتها حين تنشق

rows.speaker: ابن جبير والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk instead place the angels on the edges of the earth, guarding its borders as they descend.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير والضحاك: على حافات الأرض، ينزلون إليها يحفظون أطرافها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī argues that the singular generic al-malak is broader than the plural al-malāʾikah; Abū Ḥayyān rejects that grammatical argument.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: ما الفرق بين قولك: والملك، وبين أن يقال: والملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A definite generic singular can denote a collective but is not inherently broader than a definite plural; negative examples differ because negating every individual is stronger than negating a group.
rows.anchor: ولا يظهر أن الملك أعم من الملائكة، لأن المفرد المحلى بالألف واللام الجنسية قصاراه أن يراد به الجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular al-malak is used for lightness and can convey a group because the angels are said to occupy the sky's edges; it does not mean one angel moves between them at different times.
rows.anchor: وإنما جيء به مفردا لأنه أخف، ولأن قوله: على أرجائها يدل على الجمع

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the sky, the angels' dwelling, splits and they gather at its boundaries.
rows.anchor: يعني أنها تنشق، وهي مسكن الملائكة، فينضوون إلى أطرافها وما حولها من حافاتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In fawqahum, the pronoun may refer to the angels collectively, the throne-bearing angels specifically, or all creatures; the first uses collective singular agreement.
rows.anchor: والضمير في فوقهم عائد على الملك ضمير جمع على المعنى

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: The omitted specification after eight may mean eight angels, or, according to al-Ḍaḥḥāk, eight ranks.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن التمييز المحذوف في قوله: ثمانية أملاك، أي ثمانية أشخاص من الملائكة وعن الضحاك: ثمانية صفوف

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says God knows whether the eight means ranks or individual angels; Abū Ḥayyān omits mutually contradictory descriptions of the eight.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن، الله أعلم كم هم، أثمانية صفوف أم ثمانية أشخاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that day people are exposed for reckoning; the phrase answers the first conditional, with the day broad enough to include what follows the first blast, or directly marking the second blast.
rows.anchor: يومئذ: أي يوم إذ كان ما ذكر، تعرضون: أي للحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address in tuʿraḍūn covers all who are subject to reckoning; the timing clauses can be read as a substitution within the Resurrection-day setting.
rows.anchor: والخطاب في تعرضون لجميع العالم المحاسبين

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: A report from ʿAbd Allāh says Moses sees two presentations at Resurrection involving excuses, reprimands, and disputes, followed by a third in which records fly to right and left.
rows.anchor: وعن عبد الله: رأى موسى في القيامة عرضتان فيهما معاذير وتوقيف وخصومات

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers use the feminine verb lā takhfā; ʿAlī and several others read the masculine lā yakhfā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: لا تخفى بتاء التأنيث وعلي وابن وثاب وطلحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāfiyah refers to an inner secret or a condition that had been hidden in worldly life.
rows.anchor: خافية: سريرة وحال كانت تخفى في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person destined for Hell among the monotheists may receive the record in the right hand on display day and find it a comfort during punishment; another view delays it until leaving Hell, with faith as comfort meanwhile.
rows.anchor: أنه في يوم العرض يأخذ كتابه بيمينه مع الناجين من النار، ويكون ذلك يأنس به مدة العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The delayed-record view is argued to fit better, since someone being led to Hell would not joyfully invite others to read his book.
rows.anchor: فلا يناسب دخول النار. وهاؤم إن كان مدلولها خذ، فهي متسلطة على كتابيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If hāʾum means take, it governs the record directly; if it means come here, the record is reached through ilā. Basrans assign the following read command, while Kufans assign hāʾum.
rows.anchor: فالبصريون يعلمون اقرأوا، والكوفيون يعملون هاؤم

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers retain hāʾ al-sakt in the connected and paused forms for book, reckoning, wealth, and power, and also in mā hiyah in al-Qāriʿah.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: كتابيه، وحسابيه في موضعيهما وماليه وسلطانيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin deletes the hāʾ and silences the yāʾ; Ibn Abī Isḥāq and al-Aʿmash delete it only in connected speech, while Ḥamza does so for selected forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن: بحذفها وصلا ووقفا وإسكان الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrawī calls retaining hāʾ in connected speech an error, but Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because the transmitted reading is mass-transmitted and must be accepted.
rows.anchor: ليس كما قال، بل ذلك منقول نقل التواتر فوجب قبوله
